title: Why suffering
hookLine: the Gurus call pain a medicine and never pretend it isn't pain

lines: ONE MAN, ONE WEIGHT, ONE CLIMB.
cards: A man has been carrying something heavy for a long time, and he's sure the weight is his alone. Everyone else seems fine. Their doors look calm, their windows bright.
So he climbs up high, high enough to see the whole town at once. And from up there he sees it. Smoke from this house.
Smoke from that one. House after house, a fire burning inside. That climb is a couplet of Sheikh Farid, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib.

teach.h: FARID: A FIRE IN EVERY HOUSE.
teach.b: First, Farid up high. In paraphrase: Farid, I thought the pain was mine alone, but pain is spread through the whole world; when I climbed up and looked, I saw this same fire in house after house.
The couplet doesn't say the fire is small, or fake, or deserved. It says it's everywhere. The starting point is honesty.
Second, a line from Guru Nanak in Asa di Var that sounds upside down: dukh daaroo, sukh rog bhaiaa.

teach.h: PAIN THE MEDICINE, COMFORT THE DISEASE.
teach.b: Pain became the medicine, and comfort became the disease. Why? The line goes on, in paraphrase: when there is comfort, the Lord is not remembered.
Comfort lulls. Pain wakes. A hard week can ask what matters in an afternoon.
Third, a medicine is still bitter. The Guru doesn't say it doesn't hurt. Nobody hands someone a bitter cup and calls it delicious.
The Gurus' hymns hold real grief and real crying out; we heard one of those protests last week.

teach.h: YOUR PAIN, NOT A VERDICT ON THEIRS.
teach.b: Fourth, the medicine is for your own pain, not a verdict on someone else's. A Sikh can say of their own hard season, this woke me up.

That's very different from telling a grieving neighbor their loss is good for them. Sikh life answers other people's pain the plain way: with food, with seva, with showing up. So the Gurus give no tidy answer to why.
They give a way to stand in it: name the fire honestly, let it wake you, and don't leave anyone else alone with theirs.

how: Sikhs often meet hardship by turning to the Guru's word, saying Ardas with family and sangat, and serving others; Guru Nanak's line calling pain the medicine is often recalled in hard times.

o: pain met honestly, a bitter medicine that can wake us
proof that God has stopped caring for the world
a test you pass by never showing any grief

games.q: what's inside the teaching on suffering: tap the pairs.
p: a fire in house after house

s: calling pain a medicine means it doesn't really hurt
a medicine is still bitter; the Gurus never pretend pain isn't pain.
in Asa di Var, Guru Nanak calls comfort the disease
when there is comfort, the line says, the Lord is not remembered.
Farid thought at first that his pain was his alone
then he climbed up and saw the same fire in house after house.

games.q: you're Farid. you're sure the pain is yours alone, and everyone else looks fine. what do you do?
o: stay inside and keep it to yourself.
climb up high and look at the whole town.
decide everyone else has it easy.
games.why: he climbs, and from up there he sees the same fire burning in house after house.

practice: Let one real pain come to mind, not the biggest, one you can hold for two minutes, and name it plainly in a few words, the way Farid named his fire, without arguing or telling it it's fine.
Then gently ask whether it's waking anything up in you; if nothing comes, that's all right too. If you pray, you can hold it before God without dressing it up.
If a pain feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Why suffering. The Gurus call pain a medicine, because it wakes us when comfort lulls us, and they never pretend it isn't pain. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pain, the medicine. Guru Nanak's line in Asa di Var goes on: comfort became the disease.

carryVoice: Your line: pain, honestly. Nobody has to stand alone with their fire. See you tomorrow.
